item.title: MPs vote to fly rainbow flag at parliament for first time
item.description:
MPs vote to fly rainbow flag at parliament for first time

October 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The rainbow flag will fly at the Dutch parliament building on Sunday, Coming Out Day, after MPs overturned a decision by managers of parliament to drop the plan.
MPs backed the move by 90 votes to 36 in a vote late on Thursday night, public broadcaster NOS reported.

Parliament’s presidium, which runs its day-to-day affairs, initially agreed to the plan but changed its mind after Christian parties were told about the plan, RTL Nieuws reported on Thursday.

The orthodox Protestant SGP led the objections. “The rainbow flag is not a national flag but a flag of interest groups, which has grown into a symbol of activism,” SGP MP Diederik van Dijk told NOS.

Roll-call vote
Kati Piri, MP for opposition party Pro, then tabled a motion saying parliament should “stand up for the rights of the global LGBTI movement” and ensure “an inclusive working environment” for its staff.

Van Dijk responded by demanding a roll-call vote, in which each MP votes individually rather than by party. That meant MPs who had already gone home on Thursday had to return to The Hague.

Most MPs from D66, the VVD, CDA, PRO, PvdD, SP, ChristenUnie, 50PLUS and Volt voted in favour. The anti-immigration PVV, far-right Forum for Democracy (FVD), Denk and the SGP voted against, while MPs from JA21 and the Markuszower group were absent.

Purple Friday
The vote came on the eve of Purple Friday (Paarse Vrijdag), when schools mark LGBTI acceptance. This year it is being held in October for the first time, having been moved from December at the request of schools.

A record 3,130 schools have signed up, including 2,130 primary schools, compared with 2,890 last year, LGBTI rights organisation COC told news agency ANP.

The COC linked the rise to a survey published last month that found acceptance of homosexuality has slumped among teenagers. Only 22% of secondary school boys and 51% of girls now have a positive view, down from 40% and 78% in 2021.

item.title: MPs push for legal changes after pro-Hamas demonstration on Dam
item.description:
MPs push for legal changes after pro-Hamas demonstration on Dam

October 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

MPs are calling for a bill criminalising support for terrorist organisations to be pushed through faster, after demonstrators carried a “We support Hamas” banner onto the Dam on October 7, the third anniversary of the attacks in Israel.

Police and prosecutors judged that doing so was not illegal under current law. Police later stopped the marchers from heading towards the city’s Jewish quarter, home to the Portuguese Synagogue, the Jewish Museum and the Holocaust Names Monument.

Around 150 people were part of the group, according to Het Parool, with some chanting “Long live the 7th of October”. Some also carried a banner from the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PLFP), which is also on the EU terrorist list.

Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema described the event “shocking and distasteful” but noted that the protests were not illegal.

Protestors only have to notify a local council to hold a demonstration, and authorities can stop or intervene in one if it poses a threat to local safety or order.

Rival political figures have criticised the lack of intervention on Halsema’s part, with JA21 MP Ingrid Coenradie branding the decision to allow the protest “appalling”.

Orthodox Protestant SGP MP Diederik van Dijk submitted written questions to the justice minister David Van Weel asking why the protest was not broken up sooner.

A bill is already in parliament, submitted by Van Weel in June, proposing 3 new offences: glorifying the most serious terrorist crimes, distributing material that glorifies them, and publicly expressing support for banned terrorist organisations, which would carry a maximum sentence of 2 years in prison.

Van Weel amended the bill to meet objections from coalition party D66, which had long opposed it, so that support would only be punishable if it is aimed at winning others over to an organisation’s terrorist goals.

Peace organisation PAX has called for the bill to be scrapped, warning the law could be used against activists, journalists and protesters, and pointed to developments in the UK.

There, at least 3,070 people had been arrested by the end of April this year for showing support for Palestine Action, after the government banned the group as a terrorist organisation.

In 2024, around 320 people were arrested in Amsterdam after Halsema broke up a pro-Palestinian protest held on the same day as an October 7 commemoration on the Dam.

item.title: Maastricht area plans 30 care zones to tackle loneliness
item.description:
Maastricht area plans 30 care zones to tackle loneliness

October 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A new plan by care agencies and insurance companies aims to create 30 residential care zones in the Maastricht-Heuvelland area of Limburg, combining health services, activities and accessible living.

The plan, known as the Deltaplan Maastricht Heuvelland, aims to help older people live independently for longer and receive support and care closer to home, largely to tackle loneliness.

The initiative is a collaboration between municipalities, health insurers, residents, hospitals and elderly care advocacy agencies. Health insurers CZ and VGZ have provided €33.4 million for the project.

Nineteen of the 30 zones are currently under development, and organisers say the rest will be up and running next year.

“We have traditionally been accustomed to looking to nursing homes, but in this way, older people can continue living at home much longer, provided it is responsible,” Petra Lamberts, chair of Deltaplan, told regional news outlet L1.

The zones will also organise more activities, for example in a shared communal living room, to tackle loneliness. “Loneliness is a predictor of the need for care,” Lamberts told broadcaster NOS. “People notice minor ailments sooner when they are alone. When they take part in activities, they are distracted, and they are also encouraged to use their skills.”

Informal carers, such as family members, will also be able to hand over some of their tasks from time to time so they do not become overburdened.

A communal living room recently opened in Valkenburg, where local residents can take part in activities and meet for coffee.

The population of the region is ageing faster than the rest of the country. By 2030, one in four residents of South Limburg will be over 65.

According to Lamberts, a year of home care costs around €12,000, while a year in a nursing home costs more than €100,000.

item.title: Defence minister calls Russia “the enemy”, but policy unchanged
item.description:
Defence minister calls Russia “the enemy”, but policy unchanged

October 8, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Defence minister Dilan Yeşilgöz has started calling Russia “the enemy” rather than “the aggressor”, but says the change in wording does not mean any immediate change in national security policy.

The right-wing liberal VVD minister used the term during Thursday’s parliamentary debate on the defence budget. In a break in the debate, she told public broadcaster NOS that a rise in sabotage, drone incidents and intimidation in Europe meant the threat should be named plainly.

“It is very clear that Russia is presenting itself as the enemy,” she said. “That does not mean we are at war or that we will suddenly take a completely different approach.”

In August, the cabinet published a draft law that would give the domestic intelligence service AIVD and military intelligence service MIVD sweeping new powers against Russia, China and Iran.

A “new reality”
Yeşilgöz said Russia had long been the biggest threat to Europe, but the danger had grown into what she called a “new reality”. “Putin is testing how strong our alliance is,” she said. She added that experts had advised her to call things what they are.

The policy of investing more in defence and working closely with European allies has been in place since Russia invaded Ukraine, she said. “We were not naive before and we will not become naive now.”

In April, the AIVD said in its annual report that national security was under more pressure than at any time since the Second World War.

Oversight concerns
Under the draft law, the intelligence services would be able to designate “evident adversaries”, such as a Russian intelligence agency, and act against anyone believed to be working for them without asking a watchdog for permission first. A single new regulator would check afterwards whether the action was lawful.

The services would also be able to demand information from organisations such as banks, universities and online platforms.

The independent watchdogs that currently oversee the AIVD and MIVD have strongly criticised the plans. Hugo Hillenaar, who chairs the intelligence review committee CTIVD, told NOS last month that the changes could threaten the democratic rule of law itself.

item.title: Drugs gangs adapting as customs faces cuts, chief tells MPs
item.description:
Drugs gangs adapting as customs faces cuts, chief tells MPs

October 8, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch customs service will have to endure substantial budget cuts because it is not formally counted as part of the country’s security system, its director general has told MPs, warning of the impact cutbacks could have as criminal gangs step up pressure on the country’s ports.

Customs chief Nanette van Schelven told parliament in a position paper on Wednesday that the agency will be hit by cuts planned for government departments. It will also miss out on the extra money the cabinet has made available to strengthen the national security sector.

The agency’s role in tackling organised crime “requires continuation and intensification”, Van Schelven wrote. Customs is looking for smarter ways of working, she said, “but efficiency alone will not resolve this tension.”

Customs, which comes under the finance ministry, has a budget of almost €982 million for 2027.

New smuggling methods
Customs officers seized 19,332 kilos of cocaine in the first half of this year, up 20% on the 16,104 kilos seized in the same period of 2025, according to the paper and figures provided by customs. That is already close to last year’s total of almost 24,500 kilos.

The paper also cited more than 106 million illegal cigarettes seized in the first half of the year.

Gangs adapt quickly, Van Schelven wrote, and customs has to anticipate trends rather than rely on seizures alone. She named dropping drugs at sea for collection, soaking cocaine into other materials, chemically disguising it, and smuggling via private aircraft.

The risk of drop-offs means smaller Dutch ports need to stay alert, the paper said.

Pressure on staff
Van Schelven’s “first concern” was criminal networks’ growing willingness to use violence and the pressure they put on the organisation and individual officers.

Arrests of customs staff for corruption show how concrete that threat is, she wrote.
Measures like periodic screening take a long time to introduce, and customs needs proper resources to protect its people, the paper said.

The hearing was held by parliament’s justice committee to discuss the government’s first national threat assessment of how organised crime undermines Dutch society. MPs will debate organised crime with justice minister David van Weel later this month.

item.title: Get help with careers, homes and more at IamExpat Fair The Hague
item.description:
Partner content

Get help with careers, homes and more at IamExpat Fair The Hague

October 8, 2026

The IamExpat Fair is returning to the Grote Kerk in The Hague on Saturday November 7 with more exhibitors than ever, three international centres from across South Holland and large sections for families and health.

The IamExpat Fair, now in its 24th edition, provides advice and services of all kinds for the international community, from housing and careers to schooling and leisure, including special offers only available for attendees. A limited number of free tickets are available online, after which they cost €6, or €10 at the door.

“We have an exciting lineup of exhibitors and workshops this year in The Hague,” says events manager Claire Leunissen.

“From exhibitors specialised in preparing newcomers for the inburgering exams, to career coaches experienced in advising expats, and stocking the health & leisure section with physical and mental resources, we’re confident that services at the IamExpat Fair will help internationals thrive. ”

Workshops, presentations and centres
Experts will run workshops throughout the day on topics including buying a house and securing a mortgage, job hunting and help with lifestyle and health. Places are limited, so make sure to book your chosen sessions in advance – you can sign up here.

The Hague International Centre will have a large stand, joined by representatives from across the province, including Leiden International Centre and the Rotterdam International Center, to answer practical questions about settling in the region.

Learning Dutch and finding work
For newcomers working toward the inburgering exams, there are resources from Inburgering Online and Easy Dutch, alongside language schools including Language Institute Regina Coeli, and Bart de Pau.

Career stands and coaches include recruitment agency Undutchables and Work & Worth Coaching, while Work in South Holland will explain the state of the labour market across the region’s main industries.

Families and health
The Family & Kids section brings together several international schools, including the International School of The Hague, The British School in the Netherlands, International School Delft and Optimist International School. There is also kids’ area where families can play games together.

The Health & Leisure section is one of the largest at the fair, with exhibitors ranging from mental health services to dentists and chiropractors.

The IamExpat Fair The Hague takes place in the Grote Kerk on Saturday November 7 from 10am to 5pm. Free tickets are available online while they last; after that, entry costs €6 in advance or €10 at the door. The first 1,000 visitors receive a free tote bag.

item.title: New report says transgender law caused “profound” suffering
item.description:
New report says transgender law caused “profound” suffering

October 8, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The law governing how transgender people could change their legal gender had profound physical, psychological, and social consequences, according to a report by Radboud University released on Thursday.

Researchers conducted 28 in-depth interviews with trans and intersex people, as and studied Health Council and parliamentary papers to reach the conclusions found in the report, titled An Inhuman Law.

The report, commissioned by the education ministry, “examines how the law ​​and its conditions impacted the lives of trans and intersex people, as well as the forms of harm, coercion, and loss of autonomy they experienced”.

From 1985 to 2014, trans people had to meet a series of criteria to change their legal gender. Until 2001, they had to be unmarried, so some were forced to divorce their partners.

They also had to undergo physical adaptation “as far as medically or psychologically justified” and be permanently infertile, which meant having the uterus and ovaries or the testicles removed.

Some 2,000 people are thought to have been affected by it, the Volkskrant reported on Thursday.

“You have to negotiate with society, with doctors, and with God knows who.
And you no longer have time for yourself,” one trans woman who participated in the study said.

Junior education minister Judith Tielen said the report “helps us learn from what happened at the time”.

The bill was controversial when it was proposed in 1982. The CDA felt that without requiring physical changes, it would be too easy to change genders, which would also allow gay couples to marry and for men to avoid conscription. But D66 and PSP (which would eventually become GroenLinks and then Pro) were opposed to any surgical or medical requirements.

In 2021, the government apologised to all transgender people who were forced to accept being sterilised and to undergo body modification and take hormones if they wanted to change their gender on official documents.

The apology followed legal action by the Transgender Collective in 2019, which said that the law conflicted with the European Convention on Human Rights. In 2011, the Dutch law was also the subject of a damning report by Human Rights Watch.

item.title: Buyers get more room to negotiate as housing supply grows
item.description:
Buyers get more room to negotiate as housing supply grows

October 8, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Home buyers in the Netherlands had more choice and, in some cases, more room to negotiate over the summer, but the market remains tight, according to estate agents’ association NVM.

Almost two-thirds of homes sold by NVM agents between mid-June and mid-September went for more than the asking price, down from 71% a year earlier, the association said on Thursday.

“More supply gives home buyers a bit more breathing space,” said Lana Goutsmits-Gerssen, chair of the NVM’s housing group. “They have more choice, can more often plan a second viewing and get more room to negotiate on some homes.”

Some 39,000 existing homes were on the market with NVM agents at the end of the period, 24% more than a year ago. The average sale price was €503,000, up 1.8% year on year.

Prices in the Greater Amsterdam region rose just 0.6%, and fell slightly in the Haarlem and Leiden areas and in Zeeland. The biggest rise, 8.3%, was in southwest Drenthe.

Sales held steady at around 41,700, roughly the same as a year earlier. The NVM first reported signs of the market starting to shift in January.

Rental supply shrinks
Much of the extra supply comes from former rental homes, mainly apartments, as landlords continue to sell up. That has widened the choice for buyers but reduced the number of homes available to rent, the NVM said.

The association’s measure of market tightness, which compares the number of homes for sale with the number sold, rose to 2.8 from 2.3 a year ago. Anything below 5 counts as a tight market.

item.title: BAM buys pipeline firm A.Hak for €504m
item.description:
BAM buys pipeline firm A.Hak for €504m

October 8, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Construction company BAM announced on Thursday that it had purchased Geldermalsen-based pipelines company A.Hak for more than half a billion euros.

A.Hak specialises in underground infrastructure, including heat networks and transport pipelines.

BAM said in a press release that it had acquired the company to better position itself in the growing Dutch energy market.

The acquisition “complements our existing capabilities with specialist expertise in transport pipelines and trenchless techniques,” BAM CEO Ruud Joosten said in a statement.

The construction giant paid €504 million for the acquisition.

A.Hak operates primarily in the Netherlands but also in Belgium and the United Kingdom. It earned nearly €18 million in profits in 2025.

item.title: Alkmaar mayor defends ban on Israeli club’s fans at AZ match
item.description:
Alkmaar mayor defends ban on Israeli club’s fans at AZ match

October 8, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The mayor of Alkmaar is facing scrutiny over her decision to bar all supporters of Israeli club Hapoel Be’er Sheva from a Europa League game set to be played against AZ at the city’s AFAS Stadium on October 15.

The decision was taken, mayor Anja Schouten said, to prevent public disorder in and around the city. It follows violence surrounding Maccabi Tel Aviv’s match against Ajax in Amsterdam in November 2024, which spurred Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema to call on Alkmaar to prevent a similar situation.

Some local councillors criticised the decision in an emergency debate on Monday, NRC reported.

The Lawfare Project, a US-based pro-Israel legal group, told Dutch News it is examining possible legal action, arguing the ban is discriminatory.

Schouten told councillors last week the decision was based on public order, “not on political considerations”. Keeping groups apart was possible “with heavy deployment” around the stadium but “virtually impossible” elsewhere, particularly as visiting fans were expected to stay in Amsterdam hotels, she said.

Lawfare said that UEFA rates Hapoel’s supporters as only medium risk, and that if security cannot be guaranteed for them, then no one should be allowed to attend.

The ban is not on Israeli nationals, only on Hapoel ticket holders and on displays of support for the opposing club in the stadium, according to AZ. A spokesperson from AZ confirmed to Dutch News that no ticket sales had been made before the decision was taken.

Banning away fans from home games is common in Dutch football when authorities judge the risk too high.

In December 2024, Amsterdam barred Lazio fans from a Europa League match against Ajax over the risk of anti-Semitic and racist incidents. Enschede’s mayor reversed a similar ban on Besiktas supporters after the Turkish club called it discriminatory.

Schouten also barred Ajax fans from a cup match in January 2025 after hooligans stormed an AZ supporters’ café. UEFA normally requires clubs to offer 5% of tickets to visitors but generally accepts such bans, broadcaster NOS reported.

Dutch fans have often been on the receiving end of one-way bans. In October 2024, French authorities barred PSV fans from a Champions League match in Paris a week before kick-off, after 2,000 had already bought tickets.

Feyenoord supporters have been barred from several matches in Rome since riots in 2015 caused €8 million of damage in the Italian capital.

They were also kept out of Lille in January 2025 after a legal challenge failed at France’s highest administrative court.

Other tactics
Other host cities facing Hapoel this season have used different routes to avoid trouble.

Leuven’s mayor Mohamed Ridouani refused to host Union Saint-Gilloise’s match against the club “not even behind closed doors”, saying people could still flock to the stadium. The game will instead be played without spectators in Düsseldorf on October 22.

Turkish club Besiktas will play its home match against Hapoel in Batumi, Georgia, on November 26 with spectators present, club president Serdal Adalı said last week.

Of the three, only Alkmaar is keeping the match in its own stadium while excluding one set of fans.
